clue.text: Mocking such a boom, in a way? The opposite

indicators.note: the clue offers 'a way' placed inside the boom; the following phrase flips which piece holds which
the opposite of the stated order: the boom goes around the 'a way' rather than the other way round

parts.note: a sonic boom, so the kind of boom is sonic
RD is the standard abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a loud bang, then corrects themselves: it was the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally, 'in a way' would put the boom inside; 'The opposite' swaps the roles, so the way goes inside the boom instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A sardonic remark is grimly scornful, so the adjective is a close synonym of jeering or derisive.

clue.text: Mean to dress naughty child in blue

indicators.note: to dress means the colour word is wrapped around the child like clothing

parts.note: sky blue, so sky stands for blue
an imp is a mischievous child

explanation.surface: Someone intends to put a mischievous youngster in blue clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like a verb (intend); it is the adjective, stingy or meagre.
explanation.definitionFit: Skimpy means meagre or inadequate in amount, so it matches mean in the sense of stingy.

clue.text: English trousers tailored to be turned up

indicators.note: tailored suggests cloth being cut and reshaped, so the letters are refashioned

explanation.surface: English trousers are altered by a tailor to have turn-ups.
explanation.walkthrough: Retroussé is usually said of a nose that tilts upward at the tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Retroussé, from French, describes a nose turned up at the tip.

clue.text: One appearing in musical theatre

indicators.note: appearing in says the numeral turns up within the show's title

parts.note: Oliver! is the stage musical based on Oliver Twist
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone appears in a show at a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The Olivier is one of the National Theatre's auditoria in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Olivier is a named auditorium at the National Theatre, an example of a theatre.

clue.text: Small movie-maker at home with cutting device

parts.note: in means at home, as in staying in
a die is a tool for cutting or stamping shapes

explanation.surface: A minor film producer works from home using a cutter.
explanation.definitionFit: An indie is an independent film studio, typically a small one outside the majors.

clue.text: Peculiar pet almost causing commotion

parts.note: rum is an old British word for odd or peculiar

indicators.note: almost means the pet word stops one letter short of its full length

parts.note: a puss is a pet cat

explanation.surface: An odd household animal is stirring up a fuss at home.
explanation.walkthrough: RUM is chiefly British slang for strange. 'almost' drops the last S of PUSS to leave PUS.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumpus is a noisy disturbance or uproar, a straightforward synonym of commotion.

clue.text: Shells removed from gunners over scare

indicators.note: removing the shells strips each of the next two words of its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Artillerymen are frightened after the casings are taken from their guns.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip the outer letters from GUNNERS and OVER to get UNNER and VE.
explanation.definitionFit: To unnerve someone is to make them lose courage, close in sense to frighten.

clue.text: Earnestly seeks audience's approval

indicators.note: an audience hears rather than reads, so the word for approval is taken as heard

parts.note: praise is approval or commendation

explanation.surface: A performer anxiously hopes for the crowd's applause.
explanation.definitionFit: To pray for something is to ask for it earnestly, so it means earnestly seeks.

clue.text: Charming kind of bee?

definitions.meaning: casting charms, that is, putting under a spell
a ... bee is a contest of ... words aloud

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both casting a spell on someone and the contest in a spelling bee.

clue.text: Tree said to be less healthy on heath

indicators.note: said to be indicates the following words are heard rather than spelt

parts.note: sicker means less healthy and a moor is heath, spoken one after the other

explanation.surface: A tree is reported to be ailing more on the open heathland.
explanation.walkthrough: SICKER + MOOR, run together, sounds like the tree in many accents; 'on' just joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: The sycamore is a large maple widely planted in Britain, an example of a tree.

clue.text: Now, a death? Dying is an upset

indicators.note: upset signals that the letters of the preceding words are knocked over into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone laments how commonplace a death has become, calling dying an upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Now' at the start looks like part of the sentence; it is the definition, and the rest is fodder for 'upset'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means at the present time or in the modern era, so it stands for 'now'.

clue.text: View from one side supporting dossier

parts.note: pro means in favour of, supporting
a file is a dossier of documents

explanation.surface: A side-on look at things backs up a file of documents.
explanation.definitionFit: A profile is an outline seen from the side, such as a face drawn sideways.

clue.text: I'm under pressure to answer look hurt when rejected

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the two following words are read backwards as one run

parts.note: lo is an old exclamation meaning look
sore means hurt or painful

explanation.surface: Someone under strain is told to reply but looks wounded at being turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when rejected' turns the two words together, giving EROSOL. The definition speaks as the object itself: a spray can whose contents are held under pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerosol can holds its contents pressurised, so it could say of itself that it is kept under pressure.

clue.text: The French art crowd love a drink!

parts.note: in French 'tu es' means 'thou art', so es is French for art
a press is a dense crowd, as in the press of people
love is nil in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: A French gallery set toasts their affection with a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'art' is the old verb form (thou art), whose French is ES, not painting.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso is strong black coffee forced through ground beans, a kind of drink.

clue.text: In teams, form up waiters

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the assembled letters read from bottom to top
In puts the form word inside the teams word

parts.note: sets are groups, as in teams of players
to draw is to form, as in drawing up a plan

explanation.surface: Within the teams, the waiters are ordered to line up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' gives SDRAWETS; 'up', in a down clue, reverses it all. 'form up' looks like a parade-ground order.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewards serve passengers on ships and planes, so they are a kind of attendant or waiter.

clue.text: German town's characteristic feature: no church

indicators.note: no means the church abbreviation is left out of the word for a characteristic feature

parts.note: essence is the intrinsic quality or characteristic nature of something
CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: A guide describes a German town's defining trait: it has no church.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove CE (Church of England) from ESSENCE to leave the town; the 's of town's joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr region of western Germany.

clue.text: Mission's craft employed in making rooms trendy

parts.note: room is space, so rooms are spaces
hip means fashionable or trendy

explanation.surface: A mission's vessel is used to make cabins fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: A spaceship is the vehicle for a mission to space, the craft that flies it.

clue.text: Shopkeeper is a story-teller

definitions.meaning: one who sells goods to the public from a shop
to retail a story is to recount it, so one who retells tales

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a shop trader and one who passes on stories.

clue.text: Press boss gets workers in to make corrections

indicators.note: the workers are placed in, within the word for an editor

parts.note: ED is short for editor, the boss of a newspaper
men are workers, as in the workforce

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor brings staff in to fix mistakes.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct its errors, so the verb means make corrections.

clue.text: Grenade thrown to create disorder

indicators.note: thrown suggests the letters are tossed about and land in a new order

explanation.surface: A grenade is hurled to cause chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: To derange is to throw into disorder or disarray, so it means to create disorder.

clue.text: Ultimate race starting under arc lights

parts.note: a race is a sporting event

indicators.note: starting points to the opening letter of each of the next three words

explanation.surface: The final race of the meeting starts beneath floodlights.
explanation.definitionFit: Eventual means coming at last, so it is a synonym of ultimate or final.

clue.text: One stuck in bed's canopy gets more irritable

indicators.note: stuck in means the numeral is pushed inside the canopy word

parts.note: a tester is the canopy over a four-poster bed
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone trapped in a four-poster's canopy grows crosser.
explanation.walkthrough: TESTER is an old word for the canopy above a four-poster bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Testy means irritable, so its comparative is the same as more irritable.

clue.text: Inventor — description of his humility put up

indicators.note: put up, in a down clue, means the phrase is read upwards, from the end

parts.note: a humble person has no side, side meaning pretension or swagger

explanation.surface: A modest inventor's character is put on display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Side' is British slang for airs or pretentiousness, so a humble man has NO SIDE, reversed by 'put up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison was the American who invented the phonograph and electric light bulb.

clue.text: State regalia redesigned

indicators.note: redesigned says the letters of regalia are made into a fresh pattern

explanation.surface: A nation's crown jewels have been given a new look.
explanation.definitionFit: Algeria is a country in North Africa, an example of a sovereign state.

clue.text: Information about quartet is an assumed fact

indicators.note: about means the information word goes around the quartet

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Details on a four-piece group are taken for granted.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is British slang for information; 'given' as a noun is a premise taken for granted.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, this word is a fact or premise taken as settled for argument.

clue.text: Defer backing us with money allocated

indicators.note: backing means the small word us is run backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a spend is a sum budgeted, as in the advertising spend

explanation.surface: Someone asks to put off support for us while funds are being set aside.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend something is to postpone or put it off for a time, a synonym of defer.

clue.text: Pointed pen defining way of writing

definitions.meaning: a stylus, a sharp instrument for writing on wax
a manner of expression in prose

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an old pointed writing tool and a manner of expression.

clue.text: They may be scared by type of robbery in church offices

indicators.note: in says one piece sits inside the plural word for church posts

parts.note: a living is a church benefice, the office of a parish priest
daylight robbery is gross overcharging

explanation.surface: Clergy in their parish posts are frightened by brazen theft.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the idiom 'scare the living daylights out of someone'. Daylight robbery is a British phrase for blatant overcharging.
explanation.definitionFit: In the idiom to frighten someone badly, these are what get scared out of them.

clue.text: One making the toll double

definitions.meaning: a bell-... sounds the toll of a church bell
a dead ... is someone's exact double or lookalike

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a bell-ringer and a lookalike, as in 'a dead ringer'.

clue.text: Reptile keeping quiet in its habitat

indicators.note: keeping means the habitat word holds the quiet letter within it

parts.note: terrain is the ground or land where an animal lives
P stands for piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A reptile stays silent in its natural surroundings.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrapin is a small freshwater turtle, which is a kind of reptile.
